findings.title: Background legacy writes inherit the request context and get cancelled when the handler returns
findings.body: All four goroutines (Create l.51, Delete l.110, Update l.135, DeleteCollection l.163) build their 10s timeout as a child of the request `ctx`. `Create`/`Update`/... then return right away. The HTTP server cancels the request context once the handler finishes, and that cancels the child context too, so the legacy write races against cancellation and often gets aborted. Legacy storage then drifts from unified storage with nothing to show for it. Derive the goroutine context from `context.WithoutCancel(ctx)` (keeping the logger and identity values), then apply the timeout to that.

findings.title: Failed legacy writes are no longer logged
findings.body: The old code logged every legacy failure (`unable to create object in legacy storage`, `could not update object in legacy store`, ...). The goroutines now only call `recordLegacyDuration(err != nil, ...)` and throw the error away (l.56, l.113, l.140, l.165). If a legacy write fails or times out, no log line names the object or the cause. Add `log.Error(err, ...)` in each goroutine.

findings.title: Legacy Update reapplies the raw objInfo instead of the object unified storage stored
findings.body: Before this change, the legacy update got `&updateWrapper{upstream: objInfo, updated: obj}`, so legacy received exactly what unified storage stored. Mode 2 still does this (dualwriter_mode2.go:298, 313-316). Now the raw `objInfo` goes to legacy, so `UpdatedObject` runs the patch/transform a second time, against legacy's current copy. If the two stores differ, the results diverge. Patch-based objInfo may also not be safe to run twice, or concurrently with the response. Wrap `res` the way the old code did.

findings.title: Legacy Create gets the original obj, concurrently with the response being encoded
findings.body: The goroutine passes `obj` to `d.Legacy.Create`. Unified storage may have changed `obj` in place, or returned it as `created`, while the handler serializes the response. That is a possible data race. Legacy also never gets the name/UID that unified storage assigned, which mode 2 copies across with `enrichLegacyObject` (dualwriter_mode2.go:53). Consider passing a deep copy of `created`.

findings.title: Duration metrics are recorded under the wrong store and label
findings.body:
Four calls record against the wrong store or label:
- Create (l.45) records a unified-storage failure with `recordLegacyDuration`.
- Update (l.129) does the same.
- Delete success (l.106) passes `name` where `options.Kind` belongs, so every object name becomes its own label value (cardinality blowup).
- DeleteCollection's legacy goroutine (l.166) records with `recordStorageDuration`.

The dashboards that mode 3 rollout depends on will show wrong error rates and latencies for each store.

findings.title: Delete puts the base logger in the context, not the enriched one
findings.body: `ctx = klog.NewContext(ctx, d.Log)` stores the logger without the name/kind/method fields. Every other method stores `log`.

findings.title: Tests never check the legacy write, and their names say otherwise
findings.body: `legacyStoreMock` and `storageMock` share one `mock.Mock`. So `setupLegacyFn` in the failing Create case (l.40-42) actually programs the unified-storage failure, and the success case named "only in the unified store" also sets up a legacy expectation. The legacy write runs in a goroutine and is never awaited or asserted (no `AssertExpectations`). These tests would pass even if mode 3 stopped writing to legacy entirely, and they would not catch the context-cancellation problem.

contracts.action: Background legacy write after a successful unified-storage write (Create/Update/Delete/DeleteCollection)
contracts.equivalent_path: Mode 2 writes to legacy synchronously and copies identity across with enrichLegacyObject/updateWrapper
contracts.before_after: Before: synchronous legacy write after storage, with errors logged. After: fire-and-forget goroutine, 10s timeout derived from the request ctx, error only fed into a metric.
contracts.visible_effect: The client gets the unified-storage result straight away. Legacy may lag behind or miss the write.
contracts.failure_mode: Bounded by a 10s timeout per write, but the context is a child of the request context, which is cancelled when the handler returns, so the write can be aborted early. Failures are silent apart from the mislabeled metrics.
contracts.open_question: Does the apiserver handler chain cancel the request context when the handler returns, before the goroutine finishes?

summary: Mode 3 now writes to legacy storage asynchronously. The goroutines inherit the request context, so the HTTP server's cancellation can abort the legacy write. Their errors are no longer logged. Legacy Update gets the raw objInfo instead of the object unified storage stored. Several duration metrics are recorded against the wrong store or label. The new unit tests never check that legacy actually gets written.
